title: Internet-Delivered Modified Cue-Exposure Videotherapy for Adolescents with Binge-Spectrum Eating Disorders: A randomized controlled trial.
summary: About 18 percent of adolescents experience binge eating episodes. This means that they feel like they are losing control while eating and can’t stop. They eat more or differently than usual. Binge eating is a key feature of certain eating disorders. These eating disorders are often not recognized and remain untreated. Many affected individuals feel ashamed and don’t dare to seek help. As a result, the problem can persist for a long time—sometimes even into adulthood. Even with treatment, many adolescents continue to have binge eating episodes. A new approach using special eating exercises could help challenge the expectations surrounding a binge eating episode. This might improve treatment outcomes. Early results show that after just two sessions, binge eating episodes and other symptoms decrease. Additionally, adolescents with overweight often lose weight in the process. Different adolescents helped us design this new study. To make the eating exercises accessible to more people, we plan to offer them via video. We will combine these exercises with standard treatment to see if this approach is even more effective. We want to find out whether binge eating episodes decrease and whether adolescents feel more in control of their eating. We will also examine whether the urge to eat reduces and whether there is any weight loss after the treatment. A formerly affected young woman will serve as a study ambassador, sharing information about the study on social media. The hope is that this new approach will help reduce binge eating and overweight, ultimately protecting the long-term health of those affected. The significance of the study results will be discussed with adolescents and their parents.
conditions: Bulimia nervosa, binge-eating disorder, and atypical forms according to ICD-11

interventions.name: Three cognitive behavioral therapy sessions (treatment as usual, TAU) plus two cue-exposure sessions with binge foods focusing on the violation of dysfunctional expectations (cue exposure focusing on expectancy violation, CEEV), delivered as an internet-based video therapy.
Three cognitive behavioral therapy sessions (treatment as usual, TAU) and two supportive counseling sessions, delivered as an internet-based video therapy.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
- Presence of at least three objective BE episodes within the past three months, accompanied by clinically significant distress and/or relevant impairment in psychosocial functioning due to the BE episodes, assessed via a clinical interview (EDE-II)
- Presence of a transdiagnostic binge eating–related disorder (bulimia nervosa [BN], binge eating disorder [BED]) or atypical forms of low frequency and/or limited duration according to ICD-11 criteria, assessed via a clinical interview (EDE-II)
- Access to a webcam, microphone, and a stable internet connection
- Sufficient proficiency in German
- Residence in Germany
- Informed consent from participants and—if participants are under 18 years of age—additional consent from their legal guardians (usually both parents)
Exclusion criteria:
- Anorexia nervosa
- Acute risk of harm to self and/or others
- Severe psychopathological symptoms beyond eating disorder pathology (e.g., severe depressive episode, acute suicidality, psychotic disorder, substance use disorder, dissociative disorders, pronounced non-suicidal self-injury [NSSI], previously diagnosed borderline personality disorder, or previously diagnosed complex post-traumatic stress disorder). Mild to moderate comorbidities do not lead to exclusion as long as eating disorder pathology represents the primary condition.
- Indication for inpatient treatment
- Current eating disorder–specific interventions within a concurrently ongoing outpatient psychotherapy
- Use of medication aimed at influencing hunger, satiety, or weight regulation, or at reducing binge eating. Other medications must have been taken at a stable dosage for at least two weeks prior to randomization.
- Changes in eating behavior and body weight that are due exclusively to physical or organic causes
- Inability of participants to provide informed consent
